Text: {{c1::Anatomy}} is the study of the body's {{c2::structure}}, while {{c1::physiology}} is the study of how those parts {{c2::function}} and work together.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: anatomy asks what a part is; physiology asks what it does.

Cue: the two are usually studied together, because a structure's shape explains how it works.

Text: {{c1::Developmental}} anatomy is the study of the changes that begin in the body at {{c2::conception}} and proceed into {{c2::adulthood}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: developmental anatomy covers the whole span from conception onward, while embryology covers only its first eight weeks.

Text: {{c1::Embryology}} is the subdivision of developmental anatomy covering the first {{c2::eight}} weeks following conception.
Back Extra: Distinguish: embryology is a part of developmental anatomy, not a separate field beside it.

Text: Among the ways anatomy is studied, {{c1::surface}} anatomy is the kind used for diagnosis, and {{c1::regional}} anatomy is the analysis of specific parts of the body.
Back Extra: Cue: surface anatomy is what a clinician reads from the outside of the body, which is why it serves diagnosis.

Text: {{c1::Gross}} anatomy studies structures {{c2::large enough to see}}, while {{c1::microscopic}} anatomy studies structures {{c2::too small to see}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: gross here means large, not unpleasant.

Distinguish: macroscopic anatomy is another name for gross anatomy.

Text: {{c1::Systemic}} anatomy is the anatomy of the {{c2::organ systems}}.
Back Extra: Why: systemic anatomy is the best approach when anatomy and physiology are being studied at the same time, because a system is defined by the job its organs share.

Text: {{c1::Comparative}} anatomy is the anatomy of {{c2::nonhuman species}}, used to assist the study of the human body.
Back Extra: Ex: a bat's wing contains a radius, an ulna, and finger bones, so its structure can be read against the human arm.

Text: Bones of different species that are similar in structure are called {{c1::homologous}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: bats, birds, porpoises and people all have a radius and an ulna in the forelimb, at very different sizes.

Pitfall: homologous means similar in structure, not identical and not necessarily used the same way.

Text: The human forearm is made of two bones, the {{c1::radius}} and the {{c1::ulna}}.
Back Extra: Cue: these two are the standard reference pair in comparative anatomy, because so many species carry versions of them.

Text: An {{c1::organ system}} is a group of {{c2::organs}} that work together to perform related functions.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an organ is one structure; an organ system is the group of organs sharing a job.

Ex: the digestive system's teeth, tongue, stomach and pancreas all cooperate on digesting food.

Text: There are {{c1::eleven::number of systems}} organ systems in the human body.
Back Extra: Roster: skeletal, nervous, circulatory, respiratory, digestive, muscular, integumentary, lymphatic, urinary, endocrine, reproductive.

Text: The {{c1::skeletal}} system is made up of the bones, cartilages, ligaments and joints.
Back Extra: Why: besides giving the body shape and protecting organs in the skull and ribs, bone also produces blood cells.

Text: The {{c1::nervous}} system is composed of the brain, spinal cord, nerves and all the body's {{c2::sensory receptors}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: vision, hearing, smell, taste and touch receptors all belong to it.

Why: it regulates the other organ systems, so it is “in charge” of many processes, both conscious and unconscious.

Text: The {{c1::circulatory}} system is composed of the {{c2::heart}}, {{c2::blood vessels}} and {{c2::blood}}.
Back Extra: Why: it transports gases, nutrients, waste products and hormones, has an active role in immunity, and helps regulate body temperature.

Text: The {{c1::respiratory}} system enables the exchange of {{c2::oxygen and carbon dioxide}} between the blood and the air.
Back Extra:
Why: it also has a role in regulating the blood's pH.

Roster: lungs, respiratory passages, diaphragm.

Text: The {{c1::digestive}} system breaks food down so it can be {{c2::absorbed into the blood}}, and eliminates waste products.
Back Extra: Roster: mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, appendix, rectum.

Text: The {{c1::muscular}} system powers the movements of the skeleton and maintains {{c2::posture}} when standing still.
Back Extra:
Why: it also enables internal organs such as the heart, diaphragm, stomach and intestines to move.

Pitfall: muscle work is not only motion — holding still is active work too.

Text: The {{c1::integumentary}} system consists of the skin, hair, sweat glands, oil glands and nails.
Back Extra: Why: it protects the body, regulates body temperature, prevents water loss and aids the production of vitamin D.

Text: The {{c1::lymphatic}} system rids the body of {{c2::foreign substances}} such as bacteria, viruses and fungi.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: it is sometimes called the immune system, which is why the same organs can turn up under either name.

Roster: spleen, thymus gland, lymphatic vessels, lymph nodes.

Text: The {{c1::urinary}} system removes waste products from the blood and regulates blood {{c2::pH}}, {{c2::ion balance}} and {{c2::water balance}}.
Back Extra:
Why: it is a filter as well as a balancer.

Roster: kidneys, urinary bladder, ureters, urethra.

Text: The {{c1::endocrine}} system is made up of organs that secrete signal molecules called {{c2::hormones}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: organs whose main job is something else — the heart and stomach among them — also release hormones, so the system is wider than the obvious glands.

Text: The female {{c1::reproductive}} system produces {{c2::oocytes}} for fertilization, provides a place for {{c2::fetal development}}, and produces {{c2::milk}} for the newborn.
Back Extra: Roster: female — ovaries, vagina, uterus, mammary glands. Male — testes, penis, prostate gland and other internal organs.

Text: An {{c1::organ}} is a group of {{c2::tissues}} specialized for a particular function.
Back Extra:
Ex: the liver, lungs, kidneys, heart and skin are all organs.

Pitfall: some organs belong to more than one organ system at once.

Text: {{c1::Tissues}} are groups of {{c2::cells}} that form the various building materials of the body.
Back Extra: Cue: the ladder runs cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.

Text:
The entire human body is built from only four basic kinds of tissue:

{{c1::nervous}}

{{c1::muscular}}

{{c1::connective}}

{{c1::epithelial}}
Back Extra: Why: the body holds a multitude of organs, so it is surprising that they are assembled from so few tissue types.

Text: {{c1::Nervous}} tissue makes up the brain, spinal cord and nerves.
Back Extra: Roster: the four basic tissue types are nervous, muscular, connective and epithelial.

Text: {{c1::Muscular}} tissue enables the skeleton to move, the heart to beat, and internal organs to {{c2::push food or fluid along}}.
Back Extra: Roster: the four basic tissue types are nervous, muscular, connective and epithelial.

Text: {{c1::Connective}} tissue makes up bone and cartilage.
Back Extra: Roster: the four basic tissue types are nervous, muscular, connective and epithelial.

Text: The surface of the skin is {{c1::epithelial}} tissue.
Back Extra: Roster: the four basic tissue types are nervous, muscular, connective and epithelial.

Text: {{c1::Homeostasis}} is a state of {{c2::dynamic equilibrium}} in the body with respect to its internal environment and functions.
Back Extra: Why: homeostasis is the big idea of physiology — the organ systems spend every moment keeping the body inside its acceptable range.

Text: In the phrase dynamic equilibrium, equilibrium means {{c1::balance or stability}} and dynamic refers to {{c2::energy}}.
Back Extra: Why: the balance is not passive — holding it steady costs the body energy continuously.

Text: A {{c1::set point}} is the ideal normal value of a variable, around which homeostasis is maintained through a {{c2::normal range}} of acceptable values.
Back Extra: Pitfall: the body defends a range, not a single exact number — a variable sitting slightly off the set point is still healthy.

Text: {{c1::Stress}} is a factor that causes one or more physiological variables to move away from their {{c2::homeostatic set point}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: in physiology stress is far broader than the everyday emotional sense — it is any imbalance, internal or external.

Why: uncorrected stress means the variables stay off their set points, and health is affected.

Text: When a virus invades, the uncomfortable symptoms produced by the {{c1::lymphatic}} system are part of {{c2::restoring homeostasis}}.
Back Extra: Why: the symptoms are the response combating the virus and ridding it from the body, not the infection itself.

Text: The two organ systems responsible for deciding whether a variable is moving away from homeostasis are the {{c1::nervous}} and {{c1::endocrine}} systems.
Back Extra:
Why: having decided, they then initiate a message to correct the imbalance.

Cue: control of homeostasis comes up again and again, because it is one of the most fundamental aspects of physiology.

Text: A {{c1::control center}} receives information about a variable, determines the {{c2::set point}}, and signals a response to correct imbalances.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a control center is either the central nervous system or an endocrine gland — the receptor only measures, the control center decides.

Text: A {{c1::receptor}} is a structure that {{c2::monitors the values}} of the body's variables.
Back Extra: Distinguish: a receptor measures and reports; it cannot change anything itself.

Text: An {{c1::effector}} is a structure that can {{c2::change the value of a variable}} in response to a signal from the control center.
Back Extra: Ex: the brain cannot lower blood pressure directly, so it signals the heart, which acts as the effector.

Text: Blood pressure is detected by sensory receptors located in the {{c1::arteries near the heart}} and in the {{c1::neck}}.
Back Extra: Pathway: receptors detect the change → the brain, as control center, recognizes it → the heart, as effector, speeds up or slows down.

Text: A {{c1::negative-feedback}} system maintains homeostasis through receptors, a control center and effectors, and works by {{c2::opposing or reversing the original stress}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: negative here means opposite — the system detects a change and initiates the opposite effect.

Ex: blood glucose rises, insulin is released, cells take glucose in, and the blood level falls again.

Text: {{c1::Positive}}-feedback systems are naturally {{c2::unstable}} and escalate the imbalance.
Back Extra: Distinguish: negative feedback reverses a change and restores balance; positive feedback drives the change further.

Text: If a hormone is involved in a feedback response, the {{c1::endocrine}} system must be involved.
Back Extra: Cue: hormones are the endocrine system's signal molecules, so naming one names the system.
